opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think a lot of the most important things come from people just trying something before anyone thinks it's a good idea. If you look back at a lot of the projects I've been involved in, Spark included, they started as someone hacking on a prototype because they were curious or annoyed by a problem, not because there was a roadmap item that said "build this." If you'd had to write a proposal and get it approved, a lot of those ideas probably would have been killed early, because on paper they look risky or unclear, and it's hard to predict what will be valuable.

In research especially, the cost of trying something is often pretty low. You can build a quick version in a few days or weeks and see if it works. That's much more informative than debating it in a meeting. Once you have something real, even if it's rough, people can react to it, users can try it, and you learn things you never would have guessed. Some of the best features we've shipped came from an engineer saying, "Hey, I built this over the weekend, look what it does."

There's also a people side. If you want really strong, creative engineers and researchers, they want ownership. They want to feel they can act on their intuition. If every idea has to go through layers of approval, you lose a lot of that energy, and the best people get frustrated and leave.

Of course, it's not "do whatever you want forever." Once something shows promise, you need to invest in it properly: testing, reliability, security, especially for something people run in production. So I think of it as two phases. The exploration phase should be cheap and permissionless. The scaling phase is where you bring in more process and decide where to put real resources. The mistake many organizations make is applying the heavy process to the exploration phase, which just means fewer things get tried, and you miss the surprising wins.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts ideas that look risky or unclear on paper with quickly building a prototype to see whether they work, saying that this is more informative than debating them.

fable-5.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes from how Spark itself started, honestly. When I was a grad student at Berkeley, nobody assigned me to build a distributed computing engine. I was working with some folks who were using Hadoop, and it was painful for the kinds of iterative, interactive workloads they cared about, and I just started hacking on something. It wasn't a funded project, there was no roadmap, no one approved it. And within a few months people were using it for real things.

That experience really shaped how I think about this. The best ideas in research and in products very often don't come out of a planning process. They come from someone close to a problem noticing that something is broken or annoying, and having the freedom and the time to try fixing it. If you require a proposal, a review, a budget line, before anyone can touch anything, you filter out exactly those ideas, because at the time they start, they don't look important. Spark didn't look important. It looked like a side project.

The other piece is speed of learning. When people can just try things, you get a lot more experiments per unit time, and most of them fail, which is fine. The cost of a failed two-week experiment is tiny. The cost of never running the experiment that would have become your next big product is enormous, but it's invisible, so organizations systematically underweight it.

At Databricks we've tried pretty hard to keep that. A lot of our products, things like Delta Lake, started with an engineer or a small group who saw customers struggling with something and just built a prototype. Nobody said "go build a transactional storage layer." They saw the problem, built something, showed it to a few customers, and it grew from there. Same with a lot of what we've done around LLMs more recently. The people who are actually talking to users and building with the tools are usually ahead of whatever the official strategy says.

Now, I'd add one caveat, which is that this only works if you have people with good judgment and a strong shared sense of what the company is trying to do. Autonomy without context is just chaos. So the job of leadership is less about approving projects and more about making sure everyone understands the problems that matter and the customers we're serving. If you get that right, you can trust people to pick what to work on, and you get far better results than you'd get from any top-down process.

r001.rationale: The response says trying ideas enables faster experimentation and learning, but does not connect it to resolving speculative objections raised during a document-based discussion.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of good ideas are hard to evaluate until you actually try them. You can write a document and debate it, but sometimes a quick prototype teaches you much more. If every experiment requires approval, you lose some of those opportunities, especially ideas that sound unusual at first.

The other part is that the people closest to a problem often see opportunities that leadership doesn’t. You want them to feel that they can take initiative and show everyone what they learned. That doesn’t mean every experiment becomes a product. It means you make it easy to get evidence, and then decide together what’s worth pursuing.

r001.rationale: The response says prototypes can teach more than document debate and provide evidence, but it does not say that trying an idea resolves speculative objections raised in that discussion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s important because you can’t predict where the best ideas are going to come from. Often, someone who’s close to a particular problem sees an opportunity that isn’t obvious to the people setting the roadmap. If they can just try it, build a prototype, and show people what works, you learn much faster.

And it makes the discussion more concrete. Instead of debating an idea abstractly or trying to get approval for it, you can say, “Here’s what I built, and here’s why it might be useful.” You still have to decide what to invest in and support, but I like keeping that initial cost of experimentation very low.

r001.rationale: The response says prototyping makes discussion more concrete and avoids abstract debate, but it does not identify trying an idea as a way to resolve speculative objections raised during document-based discussion.
